title: STRO permits, TOT, and staying compliant in San Diego
excerpt: What a San Diego short-term rental needs from the city as of November 2026: the STRO license tiers and fees, TOT rates by zone, and monthly filing deadlines.

seo.title: STRO Licenses and TOT in San Diego (2026) | Cardo
seo.description: San Diego short-term rental rules as of November 2026: STRO license tiers, caps and fees, TOT rates of 11.75% to 13.75% by zone, and filing deadlines.

heroCaption: San Diego's short-term rental rules exist to protect neighborhoods and owners alike.
bodyHtml:
A short-term rental in the City of San Diego needs two things from the city: a Short-Term Residential Occupancy (STRO) license for the host, and a Transient Occupancy Tax (TOT) certificate for collecting and remitting the tax guests pay on their stays. This guide covers what each one requires as of November 2026, what they cost, and the deadlines that most often catch owners out.

As of November 2026

Figures come from the City Treasurer's STRO page (license counts as of November 6, 2026), its Taxes and Fees page, the current TOT return form, and the city's March 2025 announcement of the new TOT rates. Updated November 17, 2026: this guide previously described a Tourism Marketing District assessment on every rental; that assessment applies only to lodging businesses with 70 or more rooms.

What STRO license does a San Diego short-term rental need?

The license tier depends on how the home is used. Tier 1 covers a home rented for 20 days or fewer a year. Tier 2 covers home sharing, where the host lives on site. Tier 3 covers whole-home rentals of more than 20 days a year outside Mission Beach, and Tier 4 covers the same inside the Mission Beach Community Planning Area.

Tiers 1 and 2 have no cap. Tier 3 is capped at 1% of the city's housing units outside Mission Beach, and Tier 4 at 30% of Mission Beach's housing units. The Treasurer reported these counts as of November 6, 2026:

  • Tier 3: 4,863 licenses issued, 798 remaining.
  • Tier 4 (Mission Beach): 1,099 issued, none remaining.
  • Tier 1 and Tier 2: 135 and 2,331 issued, no limit.

Licenses belong to the host and are not transferable to another host or address. Our guide to buying or selling a home with an STRO license covers what that means at closing, and the STRO license tracker follows the Tier 3 count.

How much does an STRO license cost, and how long does it last?

Under fees in effect since March 1, 2025, a Tier 3 or Tier 4 license costs a $41 application fee plus a $1,129 license fee. Tier 1 costs $33 plus $193, and Tier 2 costs $33 plus $284. Renewals cost the same as the original. All fees are non-refundable.

Every license expires two years from the date it was issued. The city emails a renewal notice to the host 60 days before expiration.

What does a Tier 3 or Tier 4 host have to do after licensing?

The Treasurer lists these ongoing duties for whole-home hosts:

  • A two-night minimum stay for guests.
  • Use of the license for at least 90 days a year during its term.
  • Quarterly reports to the city (required only for Tier 3 and Tier 4).
  • A local contact who responds to a complaint in person or by phone within one hour.
  • An exterior notice showing the STRO license number, the TOT certificate number and contact information.

Operating without a license has been unlawful since May 1, 2023. The city says hosts who do not comply risk a notice of violation with penalties, civil penalties and license revocation.

What is Transient Occupancy Tax, and what are the current rates?

TOT is a tax on the rent a guest pays for a stay of less than a month. The guest pays it; the operator collects it and remits it to the city. Every host needs an active TOT certificate before applying for an STRO license.

Since May 1, 2025, under Measure C, the city has charged TOT at three rates set by distance from the Convention Center: 11.75% in Zone 1, 12.75% in Zone 2 and 13.75% in Zone 3, the zone closest to the Convention Center. The city's announcement states the rates apply to short-term rental properties, and it directs operators to an interactive zone map to find their zone. The previous citywide rate was 10.5%.

What changed

Many owner spreadsheets and older listings still use the 10.5% rate. A home in Zone 3 now owes 3.25 percentage points more on the same rent.

When are TOT returns due, and what happens if one is late?

Returns are monthly. According to the city's return form, a monthly remittance is on time when it is postmarked on or before the last day of the following month, so October's tax is due by November 30. The late penalty is 1% on the first day plus one third of 1% for each additional day, up to 25% of the tax due.

Hosting platforms differ in which taxes they collect and remit for which bookings. Owners whose homes also take direct or other-channel bookings should confirm with the Treasurer's TOT office (619-615-1530) which stays they must report themselves.

Does a short-term rental pay the Tourism Marketing District assessment?

Generally not. The Treasurer's Taxes and Fees page describes the Tourism Marketing District assessment as "levied on lodging businesses with 70 or more rooms in the City of San Diego," and the TOT return form limits the 2% TMD lines to those businesses. A single-home or small short-term rental operator below that threshold does not complete them.

What does Cardo handle?

For the homes it manages, Cardo handles STRO applications and renewals, quarterly reporting, the local-contact role, and monthly TOT returns for stays the platforms do not remit. The host still holds the license and the legal obligation. Owners weighing whether a home works as a short-term rental can start with a free earning estimate, or compare license and rental math in our piece on short-term versus long-term rental.

This article is general information as of November 2026, not tax or legal advice. Rates, counts and rules change; confirm current requirements with the City of San Diego Office of the City Treasurer and a qualified professional.
